new_statements.quote: 1.4. Every vowel phoneme in Arapaho is associated with one of two prosodemes; these are high level pitch and low level pitch. In the phonemic transcription hereinafter employed the former is marked by an acute accent and the latter is unmarked. Apart from the difference in relative pitch, the prosodeme of high pitch is further differentiated from that of low pitch by being correlated with greater loudness. [...] Two contiguous like vowels with like pitch constitute a long vowel, phonetically characterized by a single impulse of stress.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Arapaho with an empty rule, so nothing to agree or disagree with. Salzmann supplies the earliest phonemic statement: two-level pitch on every vowel with loudness riding on high pitch, no positional stress rule. The open_url (WALS refdb record) is only a bibliographic entry and the DOI target at journals.uchicago.edu could not be reached by automated download; the article was read from the open archive.org full text of IJAL 22(1).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Salzmann gives no word-stress placement rule. He analyzes Northern Arapaho as having two contrastive level-pitch prosodemes (high vs. low) on every vowel, marked with an acute accent, and states that the high-pitch prosodeme is additionally correlated with greater loudness. Pitch is lexically distributed (several high-pitched vowels can occur in one word, e.g. hínííwého? 'his grandmother', nih?óóθoo 'spider'), so prominence is not assigned by a positional rule. Each register has phonetic variants (he transcribes six levels), with lower variants in contour-final and extra-low in phrase-final position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; no stress degrees are recognized, only two pitch registers with phonetic sub-variants (p. 52).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 52: 'occasionally a given morpheme—besides having automatic alternant shapes as to pitch—may freely vary as to pitch from speaker to speaker or even with one speaker at different times'; contour-final and phrase-final lowering of either register; possible pitch-marking errors where 1949 field notes lacked wire recordings (fn. 8, p. 51).
new_statements.identity_note: Salzmann 1956 explicitly describes Northern Arapaho as spoken on the Wind River Indian Reservation, Wyoming (§1.0, p. 49), and uses 'Arapaho' for that dialect throughout. The Bogomolets works held by the project also treat Northern Arapaho (Wyoming). No description of Southern (Oklahoma) Arapaho was opened.

readall_conflicts: Only Salzmann 1956 among the listed works could be opened. It frames Arapaho prominence as two contrastive level-pitch prosodemes on every vowel (a tone analysis) with high pitch correlated with greater loudness, and gives no placement rule. The later material already held by the project in our check folder (Bogomolets 2020 PhD; Bogomolets 2023 'Accent and tone in Arapaho', pp. 219-221) reanalyzes the same Northern Arapaho system as a lexical accent (stress) system, with accent position unpredictable within the morpheme, rightmost accent winning in competition, a trisyllabic right-edge window, default penultimate stress, multiple primary stresses per word, and a separate lexical tone system. The two are not contradictory on the facts (both mark the same acute-accented vowels, both say position is lexical), but differ in analytic type: Salzmann = tone/pitch registers, Bogomolets = lexical accent plus independent tone. Bogomolets 2014 (MA thesis) could not be downloaded (not reachable by automated download), so its content is unverified here.

audit.recode_to: lexical (lexical/morpheme-specified accent, quantity-insensitive) with an obligatory right-edge three-syllable window and DEFAULT PENULTIMATE stress when no lexical accent falls in the window; rightmost accent wins under clash; domain = morphological word; separate tone_note: one lexical falling (HL) toneme on long vowels/diphthongs, low-density, independent of stress (Bogomolets 2023: 230-232, 245-246; 2020: 42). If our rule is kept (author's own 'pitch accent' label decides), retain tonal-OR-pitch accent but add the window/default-penult facts and cite Bogomolets as a documented contra.

sources.quote: p.42: 'although the position of stress in a given morpheme is unpredictable (i.e. Arapaho is a lexical stress language), the distribution of stresses within a morphological word can be explained with a highly constrained Directional Accent account, comprising of (i) a three-syllable window at the right edge of a morphological word, (ii) underlying accent specification for each of the morphemes within a wordform, (iii) default penultimate accent, and (iv) a Directional accent competition resolution whereby the right-most lexical accent wins.'
